claims.text: High-temperature in-situ aberration-corrected STEM can directly reveal atomic-scale rearrangements in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
High-temperature in-situ aberration-corrected STEM can assess the structural stability of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles were synthesized at ambient temperature.
Heating at 400–800 °C induces atomic-scale diffusion and rearrangement of the individual metal species in the quinary nanoparticles.
A vacuum or inert-gas environment minimizes oxidation and contamination during in-situ heating.
The high configurational entropy of the quinary alloy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
A reduced driving force for phase separation enhances the elevated-temperature stability of the nanoparticles.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will undergo minimal morphological change during heating.
Phase segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will be suppressed during heating.
Minimal morphological change and suppressed segregation would indicate high-entropy-derived thermal stability.
Comparable mono- or bimetallic nanoparticles are expected to exhibit more pronounced coarsening or segregation under identical conditions.
At sufficiently high temperatures or long heating durations, enthalpic effects may overcome entropic stabilization and cause detectable structural changes.
Kinetic effects or non-ideal mixing may produce unexpected local atomic rearrangements.
HAADF-STEM imaging can be used to monitor nanoparticle morphology and coarsening.
Spatially resolved EDX or EELS can be used to monitor the elemental distribution during heating.
Substantial phase separation or coarsening below 600 °C, comparable to simpler alloys, would refute the proposed high-entropy stabilization.
